common_name: Pink Lapacho (Pink Ipê, Purple Trumpet Tree, Ipê Roxo)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; withhold supplemental irrigation through the dry winter months to encourage the heaviest leafless bloom, since flower buds form in response to a preceding dry, cool period.

directions: Handroanthus impetiginosus (pink lapacho, ipê roxo) is a large deciduous tree native from Mexico south to Argentina, closely related to but distinct from the pale-pink-flowered H. roseus already common in Gulf Coast landscapes. Its winter-to-early-spring flower display is markedly deeper in color than either H. roseus or Tabebuia rosea: dense, rounded clusters of tubular, deep magenta to rosy-purple flowers with a yellow-streaked throat cover the bare branches for two to three weeks before the palmate leaves emerge. The bark is thick, deeply furrowed, and scaly-checkered, giving mature trunks a distinctive rugged texture even out of bloom. Timber from this species and its close relatives is sold worldwide as 'ipe,' prized for exceptional density and rot resistance in decking and marine construction. It tolerates brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F once established, making it slightly more cold-tolerant than several of its Handroanthus relatives, and is drought-tolerant once its root system matures.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun on a very sturdy support; the heavy, thick-stemmed liana needs strong anchoring from an early age.

directions: Solandra grandiflora (showy chalice vine) is a thick-stemmed tropical liana from Central America and northern South America with large, shiny, leathery leaves and bell-shaped, golden-yellow flowers that are somewhat smaller and less flared than those of the more commonly grown S. maxima. A distinguishing feature not shared by other Solandra in cultivation: this species sets globular fruit, sometimes reaching a pound in weight, with ripe flesh described as apple- or melon-like in flavor, though the unripe fruit, seeds, and green plant parts remain highly toxic. It climbs and scrambles aggressively over pergolas, walls, and large trees, and rewards a sunny, sheltered site with heavy flowering in the cooler months. All green tissue and unripe fruit contain tropane alkaloids and must be kept away from children, pets, and livestock.

planting.note: Root cuttings or plant container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this species stays more compact than other Solandra and can be grown on a modest trellis or large container support.

directions: Solandra longiflora (trumpet plant) is a coarse, woody-stemmed vine from Cuba and Hispaniola that is more compact and manageable than S. maxima or S. grandiflora, rarely exceeding 30 feet. Its most distinctive trait is a color-changing bloom: the long, narrow, trumpet-shaped flowers open pure white and shift to yellow, then to a brownish-yellow, over their second day open, so a single plant in bloom can display flowers in several colors at once. The tubular corolla is proportionally longer and slimmer than the broad chalice form of its relatives, and the fragrance is lighter and less pervasive. Like other Solandra, every part of the plant contains toxic tropane alkaloids and it should be sited away from curious pets and children.

common_name: Lemon Falls Firecracker Plant (Yellow Coral Plant)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; site where the pale flowers show up against darker foliage or hardscape, since they read less vividly from a distance than the red-flowered species.

directions: 'Lemon Falls' is a yellow-flowered sport of the standard red-flowered firecracker plant, sharing the same rush-like, nearly leafless cascading stems but replacing the coral-red tubular flowers with pale lemon-yellow to creamy-ivory blooms hung along the arching branches from late winter into fall. Occasional reverted shoots bearing the ancestral red flowers can appear on an otherwise yellow-blooming plant and may be left for a bicolor effect or pruned out to preserve the pure yellow look. Like the species, it is exceptionally heat-, drought-, and salt-tolerant once established and is a strong hummingbird draw, but its softer color makes it a useful complement, rather than a repeat, of red firecracker plantings already in a garden.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; give this hybrid more room than the species type, since its open, wide-spreading habit fills out considerably wider than it is tall.

directions: 'St. Elmo's Fire' is a larger, more vigorous hybrid selection of firecracker plant, distinguished from the straight species by an open, airy branching habit, small round leaves scattered along the stems (the species is essentially leafless), and deeper, more saturated red tubular flowers produced in heavier flushes. It matures wider than tall, eventually spreading well beyond its planted height, and blooms nearly continuously from spring into fall in warm climates. The improved branching gives it a fuller, less wispy silhouette than the species when used as a stand-alone specimen or low, informal hedge, while still sharing the same drought tolerance and hummingbird appeal.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring once temperatures stay reliably above 60°F, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a trellis, fence, or arbor to support the climbing growth.

directions: 'Stansill's Double' sets this cultivar apart from every other Allamanda already in cultivation here by producing fully double, ruffled golden-yellow flowers with multiple overlapping whorls of petals, in contrast to the flat, five-lobed single trumpets of the species and of 'Hendersonii.' The buds show a warm brownish-bronze cast before opening, and the doubled blooms tend to hold their shape and color longer on the vine than single-flowered types. Growth habit and vigor closely track the species, so it needs the same sturdy support and hard late-winter pruning to keep it in bounds and to promote the new growth that carries the heaviest bloom. As with all allamandas, the milky sap is toxic and irritating on contact.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring once nights stay above 60°F, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a trellis or fence for support.

directions: 'Chocolate Swirl' breaks from the solid golden-yellow flower color found throughout the rest of the Allamanda cathartica cultivars grown here, instead producing large trumpet flowers in a soft creamy blush-pink that deepens toward light brown-chocolate throat markings swirled through the petal base. The muted, bicolor flower reads almost as a different species against the dark, glossy foliage typical of the group, and it blooms nearly year-round in consistently warm conditions rather than concentrating bloom in the warm season alone. Culture, vigor, and toxicity are the same as for other A. cathartica selections: a vigorous vining habit needing sturdy support, hard pruning in late winter, and toxic milky sap that should be kept off skin and away from pets.
